finding: The live range of $975-$3,600 is about right. Built totals (timing chain kit + stated hours x $120-$160 per hour, the national middle rate used for this arithmetic): economy 2012 Nissan Juke 1.6L turbo $562-$778 (3.4-3.6 hours); midsize 2009 Chevrolet Traverse 3.6L V6 $1,488-$2,089 (9.0-9.2 hours); truck 2013 Ford F-150 3.5L EcoBoost $1,257-$1,667 (8.9 hours); luxury 2015 BMW 328i $1,943-$3,330 (10-15 hours). Across the four that is roughly $560-$3,330. At the top, $3,600 fits: the BMW builds to $3,330 at 15 hours, and the parts seller that gave those hours says a dealer bill can run 'upwards of $5000', so some European cars will go past $3,600. At the bottom, the only total we could build under $975 is the small four-cylinder Juke, and it understates a real quote three ways: the hours are a manufacturer campaign time (shorter than a shop bills), the low parts figure is an online sale price, and the genuine-parts figure is the chain alone because no price for Nissan's kit was found. Add the oil, seals and gaskets every one of these jobs needs and a small four-cylinder lands near the $975 floor. The outside estimates sit inside the live range: RepairPal $2,120-$2,764, Jerry $1,600-$1,800; J.D. Power's $400-$1,000 is from 2022 and is the outlier. So the floor could arguably be a little lower (about $800) for simple four-cylinder engines, but $975 is defensible. Note that the three V6 and BMW totals do not include oil, coolant, gaskets or seals, which the job always needs. How solid the labor times are: three of the four are manufacturer times for the example vehicle and the exact job (Nissan 3.4-3.6 hours for the Juke chain and guides; GM 9.0-9.2 hours for the Traverse; Ford 8.9 hours for the F-150 primary chain, including diagnosis). These are warranty or campaign times, the low end of what shops bill. The BMW figure is a parts seller's statement that dealers charge 10-15 hours, not a published flat-rate time. Caveats on parts: the Juke genuine figure is the chain only; the F-150 genuine figure is the primary chain plus three guides added up from a catalog page that does not say which engine each part fits, with no tensioner, so it is understated; the two GM dealer catalogs show different list prices for the same chain package ($585.51 and $616.95) and neither page confirms 2009 Traverse fitment (the GM bulletin does name that part number for the engine); the BMW prices are parts-seller kit prices, one kit's contents were not shown, and no BMW dealer list price was loaded. What the unit leaves out matters here: cam phasers or VVT gears are often replaced with the chain (Ford allows 10.0 hours to replace all four on the 2017-2018 F-150 3.5L, and genuine units cost several hundred dollars each), and that pushes a quote well above these totals.
extras: A quote almost always adds engine oil and a filter, coolant, a front cover gasket or sealant, valve cover gaskets and a front crankshaft seal, because all of these are disturbed to reach the chain. Shops often recommend replacing the water pump at the same time where it sits behind the timing cover, and the cam phasers or VVT gears and their solenoids if they rattle or have set fault codes; these can add several hundred dollars or more. A diagnosis fee is common, since the visit usually starts with a rattle on start-up or a check engine light. On some all-wheel-drive and transverse V6 vehicles the engine has to be lowered or removed, which adds labor, and the air conditioning may need to be recharged. If the chain has already jumped or broken, bent valves or other internal engine damage is a separate and much larger repair. Shop supplies and sales tax are extra.
